processing: Mainly steamed sencha, with deep-steamed fukamushi increasingly common. Most first-flush leaf is shaded for about a week before picking in the kabuse manner.
harvest_season: First flush comes earlier than in Shizuoka, making this one of Japan's early-season areas. The northern hill zone around Nochidake is known for the higher grades.
appearance_dry: As with other sencha, fine dark-green needles, shorter and more broken in deep-steamed lots.
appearance_liquor: A clear young green, with more depth and some cloud when deep-steamed.
appearance_wet: Soft bright green leaf, finer and more broken in fukamushi.
taste_profile: A fresh, clean aroma with a rich sweetness; Yutakamidori fukamushi is dense and full, while Saemidori is sweet and savoury with little astringency.

brewing.notes: Fukamushi needs a shorter first steep, around 40 seconds, and a fine-mesh pot, as its small particles cloud the cup and clog a coarse filter.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's crop, and new tea reaches the market earlier than Shizuoka's. Since April 2017 the name also covers Ei and Kawanabe tea from Minamikyushu, so it is a wide label now: look for the cultivar, the steaming style and the district.
description:
Chiran-cha is the green tea of Minamikyushu in Kagoshima, the largest tea-growing municipality in Japan. Kagoshima as a whole overtook Shizuoka in crude tea output for 2024, for the first time since prefectural records began in 1959. This is a big, modern, well-run tea region, and an early one.

The gardens stand on volcanic soils, shirasu with black andosol above, which are acidic and free-draining: bad for many crops, but good for tea. The northern hills use their cool nights for higher grades, while the flatter centre and south rely on large machines. Most first-flush leaf is shaded for about a week before picking.

The four main cultivars explain much of the range. Yutakamidori gives the rich deep-steamed style, Yabukita is the balanced standard, Saemidori is sweet and vivid in colour, and Asatsuyu is the rare one, nicknamed natural gyokuro. Single-cultivar lots are the best way to taste the difference, side by side at about 70°C.

Check the cultivar and steaming style on the pack more than the place name. Fukamushi brews fast and cloudy, which is normal, not a fault.
history:
A local tale says Heike refugees began growing tea in the northern hills in the Kamakura period, and a monument marks it, but that remains tradition. Real cultivation begins in 1872, when villagers cleared land released by the Sata Shimazu family. A tea guild then brought in experts and learned Uji methods.

Machinery arrived from 1920, and sales trips to Nagasaki, Fukuoka and Korea spread the name. In 1934 a black tea factory was set up with prefectural backing, and in 1938 black tea was made and presented for the emperor. Import liberalisation undercut that trade in the 1960s, and farmers moved to green tea.

The regional brands were merged in April 2017, when Ei and Kawanabe tea took the Chiran name.
